'''Jainendra K. Jain''' (born January 17, 1960) is an [[Indian-Americans|Indian-American]] [[physicist]] and the Evan Pugh University Professor and the Eberly Chair in [[Physics]] at the [[Pennsylvania State University]]. He received the [[Oliver E. Buckley Prize]] of the [[American Physical Society]] in 2002, was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2021, and was selected Foreign Fellow of the [[Indian National Science Academy]] in 2024.<ref name="acad">{{Cite web|url=https://science.psu.edu/physics/people/jainendra-k-jain|title=Jainendra K Jain — Penn State Department of Physics|website=www.phys.psu.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-02-24}}</ref> He was the co-recipient of 2025 [[Wolf Prize in Physics]] along with [[James P. Eisenstein]] and [[Mordehai Heiblum]].<ref>[https://wolffund.org.il/jainendra-k-jain/ Wolf Prize in Physics 2025]</ref> Jain is known for his theoretical work on [[many-body theory|quantum many body system]]s, most notably for postulating particles known as the [[composite fermion]]s.

==Biography==
Jain received his primary, middle and high school education in a government school in the rural village of [[Sambhar Lake Town|Sambhar]], [[Rajasthan]],<ref name="profile">{{cite journal|last1=Ahmed |first1=Farooq |title=Profile of Jainendra K. Jain|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |date=2022 |volume=119 |issue=30 |article-number=e2208671119 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2208671119 |doi-access=free |pmid=35858393 |pmc=9335342 |bibcode=2022PNAS..11908671A }}</ref><ref name=":0" /> located at the eastern margin of Thar desert in India. He received bachelor's degree at [[Maharaja College, Jaipur]],<ref name="acap">{{cite web|title=Array of contemporary American Physicists|url=https://history.aip.org/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?jainj|publisher=American Institute of Physics|accessdate=20 October 2010}}{{Dead link|date=September 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> his master's degree in physics at [[Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur]]<ref name="acap"/> and PhD at the [[Stony Brook University]],<ref name="acap"/> where he worked with Profs. Philip B. Allen and [[Steven Kivelson]]. After post-doctoral positions at the [[University of Maryland]] and the [[Yale University]] he returned to the [[Stony Brook University]] as a faculty member in 1989. In 1998, he moved to the [[Pennsylvania State University]]<ref name="acad" /> as the first [[Erwin Wilhelm Müller|Erwin W. Mueller]] Professor of [[Physics]].

In 2026 Jain was appointed Director of Lodha Theoretical Physics Institute, Mumbai.

Jain is a quantum physicist in the field of [[Condensed-matter physics|condensed matter theory]] with interests in strongly interacting electronic systems in low dimensions. As the originator of the exotic particles called [[composite fermions]], he pioneered and developed the composite fermion theory of the [[fractional quantum Hall effect]] and unified the fractional and the integral [[Quantum Hall effect|quantum Hall effects]]. His writings include a monograph ''Composite Fermions'',<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cambridge.org/us/academic/subjects/physics/condensed-matter-physics-nanoscience-and-mesoscopic-physics/composite-fermions?format=HB&isbn=9780521862325#0A8kV02h7QDWUTxF.97|title=Composite fermions|last=|first=|date=|website=Cambridge University Press|language=en|access-date=2018-02-24}}</ref> published in 2007 by the [[Cambridge University Press]]. He co-edited with [[Bertrand Halperin]] a book ''Fractional Quantum Hall Effects: New Developments,''<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Halperin |first1=Bertrand I. |last2=Jain |first2=Jainendra K. |url=https://worldscientific.com/worldscibooks/10.1142/11751|title=Fractional Quantum Hall Effects: New Developments |date=2020 |doi=10.1142/11751 |arxiv=2011.13488 |isbn=978-981-12-1748-7 }}</ref> published in 2020 by [[World Scientific]].<ref name="profile"/>

Because of injuries sustained in a childhood accident, Jain walks with the aid of a prosthesis.<ref name="profile"/><ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=2025-05-02 |title=‘For us physicists, beauty is a new idea that unifies and explains’ |url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/lifestyle/art-culture/for-us-physicists-beauty-is-a-new-idea-that-unifies-and-explains-101746172653378.html |access-date=2025-12-19 |work=Hindustan Times |language=en-us}}</ref> After being awarded the [[Wolf Prize in Physics]], he recounted his journey as: “Looking back, it is hard to believe how incredibly fortunate I have been. Growing up in a poor village in India, traumatized by an accident that left me on crutches with a lifelong disability, I did not think I would ever walk again or attend college, let alone pursue my dream of becoming a physicist.”<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.psu.edu/news/eberly-college-science/story/jainendra-jain-named-2025-wolf-prize-laureate-physics|title=Jainendra Jain named 2025 Wolf Prize laureate in physics}}</ref> He credits [[Jaipur Foot]] with enabling him to continue education.<ref name="profile"/>
==Research==

Jain predicted that when two-dimensional electrons are subjected to a large magnetic field, they dress themselves with an even number of quantized vortices  to form emergent particles termed [[composite fermions]].<ref name="Jain-CF">{{Cite web|title=Composite-fermion approach for the fractional quantum Hall effect|author=J. K. Jain|date=1989|url=http://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.63.199|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.63.199|website=Physical Review Letters}}</ref> Composite fermions are pictured as electrons dressed with magnetic flux quanta, and are predicted to experience a substantially reduced magnetic field.  Thus, the strongly correlated 2D electrons in a high magnetic field become weakly interacting composite fermions at a reduced magnetic field. Composite fermions correctly predict the rich phenomenology of this system originating from a variety of strongly correlated states of electrons, including the fractional quantum Hall states, the Fermi-liquid like metallic states, superconductor-like paired states, and crystal states.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Olle Heinonen |date=1998 |title=Composite fermions: a unified view of the quantum Hall regime |url=https://www.amazon.in/Composite-Fermions-Unified-Quantum-Regime/dp/9812384138 |website=World Scientific}}</ref><ref name="Stormer-Tsui-review">{{Cite web |author=H. L. Stormer; D. C. Tsui |date=2007 |title=Composite fermions in the fractional quantum Hall effect |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1002/9783527617258.ch10 |website=Perspectives in Quantum Hall Effects |doi=10.1002/9783527617258.ch10}}</ref><ref name="Jain-review">{{Cite web|title=Thirty Years of Composite Fermions and Beyond|author=J. K. Jain|date=2020|website=Fractional Quantum Hall Effects: New Developments|url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/9789811217494_0001|doi=10.1142/9789811217494_0001}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author=B.I. Halperin |date=2020 |title=The Half-Full Landau Level |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/9789811217494_0001 |website=Fractional Quantum Hall Effects: New Developments |doi=10.1142/9789811217494_0001}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author=M. Shayegan |date=2020 |title=Probing Composite Fermions Near Half-Filled Landau Level |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/9789811217494_0001 |website=Fractional Quantum Hall Effects: New Developments |doi=10.1142/9789811217494_0001}}</ref>

Jain theorized that the integer quantum Hall effect of composite fermions carrying 2p flux quanta shows as the fractional quantum Hall effect of electrons at fractions n/(2pn±1), where n and p are integers. These fractions, along with their hole partners 1 - n/(2pn±1), termed the Jain sequences, account for nearly all known fractional quantum Hall states, called the Jain states. Experimental evidence has been reported for four species of composite fermions, those with 2, 4, 6, and 8 flux quanta attached.<ref>{{Cite web |author=W. Pan, H.L. Stormer, D. C. Tsui, L.N. Pfeiffer, K.W. Baldwin, K.W. West |date=2002 |title=Transition from an electron solid to the sequence of fractional quantum Hall states at very low Landau level filling factor |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.88.176802 |website=Phys. Rev. Lett. |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.88.176802}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author=Y. Huang, W. Hussain, S.A. Myers, L.N. Pfeiffer, K.W. West, K.W. Baldwin, G.A. Csathy |date=2024 |title=Evidence for Topological Protection Derived from Six-Flux Composite Fermions |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-45860-5}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Correlated states of 2D electrons near ν = 1/7|author=Y. J. Chung, D. Graf, L.W. Engel, K.A. Villegas Rosales, P.T. Madathil, K.W. Baldwin, K. W. West, L. N. Pfeiffer, and M. Shanegan|date=2022|url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.128.026802|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.128.026802}}</ref>

Jain also constructed ansatz wave functions<ref name="Jain-CF" /> for the fractional quantum Hall states, which were shown by him and his collaborators to be extremely accurate.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Jain |first=Jainendra K. |date=1997 |title=Composite fermions in the Hilbert space of the lowest electronic Landau level |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0217979297001301 |doi=10.1142/S0217979297001301}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Band structure of the fractional quantum Hall effect|author=Gautam Dev; J. K. Jain|date=1992|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.2843|url=http://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.2843}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author=A. C. Balram; A. Wójs; J. K. Jain |date=2013 |title=State counting for excited bands of the fractional quantum Hall effect |url=https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.88.205312 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.88.205312}}</ref> They demonstrated that the excited composite fermions, also called "quasiparticles", exhibit fractional charge and anyon statistics.<ref>{{Cite web |author=G. S. Jeon; K. L. Graham; J. K. Jain |date=2004 |title=Berry phases for composite fermions |url=https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.70.125316 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.70.125316}}</ref> They generalized the composite-fermion framework to include the spin (or valley) degree of freedom<ref>{{Cite web |author=X. G. Wu; G. Dev; J. K. Jain |date=1993 |title=Mixed-spin incompressible states in the fractional quantum Hall effect |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.153 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.71.153}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author=K. Park; J. K. Jain |date=1998 |title=Phase diagram of the spin polarization of composite fermions |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.80.4237 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.80.4237}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author=Y. Zhang; A. Wójs; J. K. Jain |date=2016 |title=Landau-level mixing and particle-hole symmetry breaking |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.117.116803 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.117.116803}}</ref> and to bilayers,<ref>{{Cite web |author=V. W. Scarola; J. K. Jain |date=2001 |title=Phase diagram of bilayer composite fermion states |url=https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.64.085313 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.64.085313}}</ref> and successfully predicted the phase diagram of composite-fermion crystals.<ref>{{Cite web |author=A. C. Archer; K. Park; J. K. Jain |date=2013 |title=Competing crystal phases in the lowest Landau level |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.111.146804 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.111.146804}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author=J. Zhao; Y. Zhang; J. K. Jain |date=2018 |title=Crystallization in the fractional quantum Hall regime induced by Landau-level mixing |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.121.116802 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.121.116802}}</ref> They further showed that the residual interactions among composite fermions can cause pairing of composite fermions at even-denominator fractions in higher Landau levels,<ref>{{Cite web |author=A. Sharma; S. Pu; A. C. Balram; J. K. Jain |date=2023 |title=Fractional quantum Hall effect with unconventional pairing in monolayer graphene |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.130.126201 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.130.126201}}</ref> in wide quantum wells,<ref>{{Cite web |author=A. Sharma; A. C. Balram; J. K. Jain |date=2024 |title=Composite-fermion pairing at half- and quarter-filled lowest Landau level |url=https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.109.035306 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.109.035306}}</ref> or with large Landau-level mixing.<ref>{{Cite web |author=T. Zhao; A. C. Balram; J. K. Jain |date=2023 |title=Composite fermion pairing induced by Landau-level mixing |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.130.186302 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.130.186302}}</ref>. Jain also is the originator the "parton" construction,<ref>{{Cite web |author=J. K. Jain |date=1989 |title=Incompressible quantum Hall states |url=https://journals.aps.org/prb/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevB.40.8079 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevB.40.8079}}</ref> which generates candidate fractional quantum Hall states beyond the Jain sequences and includes non-Abelian states.<ref>{{Cite web |author=X.-G. Wen |date=1991 |title=Non-abelian statistics in the fractional quantum Hall states |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.66.802 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.66.802}}</ref>

The '''Lodha Theoretical Physics Institute''' ('''LTPI''') is a private physics research centre located in [[Mumbai]],<ref>{{cite news |title=Lodha Foundation unveils theoretical physics institute to promote fundamental research |url=https://www.thehindu.com/education/lodha-foundation-unveils-theoretical-physics-institute-to-promote-fundamental-research/article71030050.ece |work=The Hindu |location=Chennai, India |date=27 May 2026 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Lodhas to launch theoretical physics institute in Mumbai |url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/cities/mumbai-news/lodhas-to-launch-theoretical-physics-institute-in-mumbai-101773774662711.html |work=Hindustan Times |date=27 March 2026 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Lodha Foundation launches India's first privately funded theoretical physics institute; aims to attract global scientists |url=https://news.careers360.com/lodha-foundation-launches-india-first-privately-funded-theoretical-physics-institute-aims-to-attract-global-scientists-ltpi |work=Careers360 News |date=27 May 2026 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> and is led by Jain.<ref>{{cite news |last=McCormick |first=Gail |title=Penn State physicist Jainendra Jain to lead new institute in India |url=https://science.psu.edu/news/jainendra-jain-lead-new-institute |work=Penn State Eberly College of Science |date=17 March 2026 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref> It is India's only private physics research institute, inaugurated on May 27, 2026, in Mumbai.<ref>{{cite news |last=Sharma |first=Surabhi |title=Lodha Foundation sets up theoretical physics institute |url=https://theprint.in/india/lodha-foundation-sets-up-theoretical-physics-institute/2943226/ |work=ThePrint |date=27 May 2026 |access-date=2 June 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Cartwright |first=Jon |title=Lodha Foundation unveils plans for India's first privately funded physics institute |url=https://physicsworld.com/a/lodha-foundation-unveils-plans-for-indias-first-privately-funded-physics-institute/ |work=Physics World |date=2 June 2026 |access-date=10 June 2026}}</ref>

==Honors==
* Fellow, [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]], 1991.<ref name="acad" />
*Fellow, [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]], 1997.<ref name="acad" />
*Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]], 1997.<ref name="acad" /> Citation: "''For the "Composite Fermion" theory of the fractional quantum Hall effect.''"
*Appointed [[Erwin Wilhelm Müller|Erwin W. Mueller]] Professor of Physics, [[Pennsylvania State University]], 1998.<ref name="acad" />
*[[Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize|Oliver E. Buckley Prize]] awarded by the [[American Physical Society]] for a most important contribution to the advancement of knowledge in Condensed Matter Physics, 2002, along with [[Nicholas Read]] and [[Robert Willett]].<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date= |title=Buckley Prize |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Jain&first_nm=Jainendra&year=2002 |access-date=2018-02-24 |website=www.aps.org |language=en}}</ref> Citation: "''For theoretical and experimental work establishing the composite fermion model for the half-filled Landau level and other quantized Hall systems''"
*Elected member of [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AAAS Fellow |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/jainendra-kumar-jain}}</ref> Citation: "''Evan Pugh University Professor and Erwin W. Mueller Professor of Physics. Predicted that electrons in the factional quantum Hall effect regime capture quantized vortices to form new particles, which he named composite fermions. Subsequently observed, composite fermions brought clarity to the subject and spawned new lines of theoretical inquiries and elegant new experiments.''"
*Distinguished Alumnus Award of [[IIT Kanpur]], 2010.<ref name="acad" />
*Fellow, [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], 2011.<ref name="acad" />
*Appointed [[Evan Pugh]] University Professor, named after the first President of [[Pennsylvania State University]], 2012.<ref>{{cite web |title=Evan Pugh University Professors |url=https://research.psu.edu/faculty-honors/evan-pugh-university-professors/}}</ref>
*Elected to [[National Academy of Sciences]], 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2021 NAS Election |url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426172730/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=26 April 2021}}</ref>
*Appointed Holder of Eberly Family Chair, [[Pennsylvania State University]], 2023.<ref name="acad" />
*Elected Foreign Fellow of the [[Indian National Science Academy]], 2025.<ref name="INSA">{{cite web |title=INSA Foreign Fellows elected |url=https://insaindia.res.in/recent-elected-fellows/}}</ref> Citation: "''Prof Jain predicted a new class of exotic particles, which he named “composite fermions,” and explained the fractional quantum Hall effect as the integer quantum Hall effect of composite fermions. In doing so, he accomplished a unification of the fractional and the integer quantum Hall effects, two Nobel prize winning phenomena. His discovery of composite fermions is recognized as a singular and transformative development in the realm of condensed matter physics.''"
*[[Wolf Prize in Physics]], 2025 together with [[James P. Eisenstein]] and [[Mordehai Heiblum]] for "For advancing our understanding of the surprising properties of two-dimensional electron systems in strong magnetic fields".<ref>[https://wolffund.org.il/jainendra-k-jain/ Wolf Prize in Physics 2025]</ref>
